Theorems and special lines in the triangle

Three sticks do not always make a triangle. The largest angle always lies opposite the longest side. And in every triangle there are four kinds of lines that meet in one single point as if by magic. In this chapter you learn these theorems, justify them and construct the special lines.

8 LESSONS2 UNITS3 LABS
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • apply and justify the base angle theorem in the isosceles triangle
  • use the side–angle relationship and the triangle inequality
  • construct perpendicular bisectors, angle bisectors, altitudes and medians
  • know what their points of intersection mean: circumcircle, incircle, orthocentre, centroid

$\alpha = 40^\circ$ and $\beta = 70^\circ$. How big is $\gamma$?

$180^\circ - 110^\circ = 70^\circ$

How far is the midpoint of a 6 cm line segment from its end points?

3 cm each.

A right angle is halved exactly. How big is each half?

$45^\circ$

How many lines of symmetry does an isosceles triangle have that is not equilateral?

One, it goes through the apex.

UNIT 14 LESSONS

1Base angles, sides and angles

With 3, 4 and 8 cm it does not work: the two short straws are only 7 cm long together, they do not reach each other. With 3, 4 and 5 cm it works. And the largest angle always lies opposite the longest straw.

A triangle with two sides of equal length is called isosceles. The equal sides are the legs, the third is the base. The angles at the base are called base angles.

Why the base angle theorem holds: join the apex $C$ to the midpoint $M$ of the base. The triangles $AMC$ and $BMC$ agree in all three sides: $\overline{AC} = \overline{BC}$ (legs), $\overline{AM} = \overline{MB}$ (midpoint), $\overline{MC}$ belongs to both. By SSS they are congruent, so the angles at $A$ and $B$ are equal as well.

KEY POINT · THREE THEOREMS ABOUT TRIANGLES

Base angle theorem: if a triangle is isosceles, then its base angles are equal. (The converse holds too.)

Side–angle relationship: if one side is longer than another, then the larger angle lies opposite it.

Triangle inequality: in every triangle two sides together are longer than the third: $a + b > c$, $a + c > b$, $b + c > a$.

Quick check: for the triangle inequality it is enough to compare the two shorter sides with the longest.

Equilateral: all sides equal, so all angles are equal: $60^\circ$ each.

INTERACTIVE · THREE STICKS

Set three lengths. The longest side and its angle light up orange, the shortest and its angle blue. Make two sides equal.

EXAMPLE 1 · BASE ANGLES

In an isosceles triangle one base angle is $70^\circ$. How big is the angle at the apex?

Both base angles are $70^\circ$. That leaves $180^\circ - 2 \cdot 70^\circ$ for the apex.

$40^\circ$

EXAMPLE 2 · ORDERING THE SIDES

In a triangle $\alpha = 30^\circ$ and $\beta = 100^\circ$. Put the sides in order of length.

$\gamma = 50^\circ$. Largest angle $\beta$, so $b$ is the longest side. Smallest angle $\alpha$, so $a$ is the shortest.

$a < c < b$

EXERCISES

Isosceles triangle: calculate the missing angles. a) base angle $55^\circ$   b) angle at the apex $100^\circ$   c) angle at the apex $90^\circ$

a) apex $70^\circ$   b) base angles $40^\circ$ each   c) base angles $45^\circ$ each

Is there a triangle with these sides? a) 5 cm, 6 cm, 12 cm   b) 7 cm, 7 cm, 13 cm   c) 2 cm, 3 cm, 5 cm

a) no, $5 + 6 < 12$   b) yes, $7 + 7 > 13$   c) no, $2 + 3 = 5$: the sticks lie flat.

In a triangle $a = 5$ cm, $b = 7$ cm, $c = 4$ cm. Which angle is the largest, which the smallest?

Largest angle opposite $b$: $\beta$. Smallest opposite $c$: $\gamma$.

Two sides of a triangle are 4 cm and 9 cm long. Between which values must the third side lie?

Longer than $9 - 4 = 5$ cm and shorter than $9 + 4 = 13$ cm.

Justify: in a right-angled triangle the side opposite the right angle is always the longest.

At most how big can the other two angles be?

The other two angles add up to $90^\circ$, so each is smaller than $90^\circ$. The right angle is the largest, so by the side–angle relationship the longest side lies opposite it.

TEST YOURSELF!

Isosceles, base angle $70^\circ$. Angle at the apex?

$180^\circ - 140^\circ$

Isosceles, apex $100^\circ$. How big is a base angle?

$80^\circ : 2 = 40^\circ$

Two sides are 4 cm and 9 cm. The third must be shorter than how many cm?

$4 + 9 = 13$

UNIT 24 LESSONS

2Special lines in the triangle

All points that are the same distance from two houses lie on a straight line: the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them. If you draw the perpendicular bisectors of all three sides, they meet in one point. That is where the playground belongs.

In every triangle there are four kinds of special lines, three of each kind. Amazingly, the three lines of one kind always meet in one single point.

For constructions there are fixed ways of saying things: you construct the perpendicular bisector, you bisect an angle, and you drop a perpendicular from a point to a line.

KEY POINT · SPECIAL LINES

Perpendicular bisector: stands at right angles on the midpoint of a side. Intersection $U$: centre of the circumcircle, the same distance from all corners.

Angle bisector: divides an angle into two equal parts. Intersection $I$: centre of the incircle, the same distance from all sides.

Altitude: the perpendicular from a corner to the opposite side (or its extension). Intersection $H$: orthocentre.

Median: joins a corner to the midpoint of the opposite side. Intersection $S$: centroid.

Perpendicular bisector with compasses: draw arcs about both end points with the same radius (more than half the segment). Join the two points of intersection.

Bisecting an angle: draw an arc about the vertex that cuts both arms. About these two points draw arcs of equal size. Join their intersection to the vertex.

INTERACTIVE · FOUR KINDS, FOUR POINTS

Choose a kind of line and drag the corners. Make the triangle obtuse: where do $U$ and $H$ end up?

EXAMPLE 3 · THE PLAYGROUND

Where must the playground be that is the same distance from three houses?

The same distance from two houses: on their perpendicular bisector. The same distance from all three: on all three perpendicular bisectors.

at the circumcentre $U$

EXAMPLE 4 · A ROUND FLOWER BED

A round flower bed, as large as possible, is to go in a triangular garden. Where is its centre?

The bed has to touch all three sides, its centre is the same distance from all sides.

at the incentre $I$, the intersection of the angle bisectors

EXERCISES

Draw a triangle with $c = 7$ cm, $b = 5$ cm, $a = 6$ cm. Construct the three perpendicular bisectors and the circumcircle.

The three perpendicular bisectors meet at $U$, and the circle about $U$ through $A$ also goes through $B$ and $C$. The radius is about $3.6$ cm.

Which line is meant? a) It goes through a corner and is perpendicular to the opposite side.   b) It goes through the midpoint of a side and through the opposite corner.   c) It goes through the midpoint of a side and is perpendicular to it.

a) altitude   b) median   c) perpendicular bisector

Cut a triangle out of card. Construct the medians and try to balance the triangle on the tip of a pencil at their intersection.

It works at the centroid $S$. It divides each median so that the piece towards the corner is twice as long as the piece towards the midpoint of the side.

Where is the circumcentre in an acute, a right-angled and an obtuse triangle? Try it out in the widget.

Acute: inside. Right-angled: exactly on the longest side, at its midpoint. Obtuse: outside.

In an equilateral triangle all four special points coincide. Why? What is special in an isosceles triangle?

In the equilateral triangle every perpendicular bisector is at the same time an angle bisector, an altitude and a median, namely a line of symmetry. In the isosceles triangle this only holds for the line through the apex: all four points lie on the line of symmetry.

TEST YOURSELF!

How many perpendicular bisectors does a triangle have?

Three, one for each side.

How many of the four intersections $U$, $I$, $H$, $S$ always lie inside, in every triangle?

$I$ and $S$. $U$ and $H$ can lie outside.

An angle of $60^\circ$ is bisected. How big is each half?

$30^\circ$

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

A gable is an isosceles triangle. The angle at the ridge is $110^\circ$. How steep is the roof, that is, how big are the base angles?

$(180^\circ - 110^\circ) : 2 = 35^\circ$

Connecting with chapter 3.1: justify with the angle sum theorem: in an equilateral triangle every angle is $60^\circ$.

All sides are equal, so by the base angle theorem all angles are equal. Three equal angles make $180^\circ$: each is $60^\circ$.

Three villages are to share one radio mast that is the same distance from all of them. The villages lie almost on one line. Why is that unfavourable?

The triangle is then very obtuse. The circumcentre lies far outside, and the circumcircle is huge: the mast would be far away from all of them.

A path from $A$ to $C$ is 5 km long directly. Via $B$ it is 3 km to $B$ and 4 km from $B$ to $C$. Why is the detour longer? Can a detour ever be shorter?

Triangle inequality: $3 + 4 > 5$. A detour via a third point is never shorter than the straight path, at most the same length, if $B$ lies on the segment.

EXCURSIONA DISCOVERY

The Euler line

The four special points of a triangle had been known since antiquity. But only in 1765 did the Swiss mathematician Leonhard Euler discover something surprising: the orthocentre $H$, the centroid $S$ and the circumcentre $U$ lie on one common straight line in every triangle.

Today this line is called the Euler line. What is more: $S$ always lies between $H$ and $U$, in such a way that the distance from $H$ to $S$ is twice the distance from $S$ to $U$. Only the incentre $I$ does not join in. In general it does not lie on the line.

Try it out: in the lab “Euler, Feuerbach and Napoleon” you can see the line and move the corners. Are there triangles in which all four points coincide?

Yes, in the equilateral triangle $U$, $I$, $H$ and $S$ coincide. Then there is no unique Euler line.

Source: Leonhard Euler, “Solutio facilis problematum quorundam geometricorum difficillimorum”, Novi Commentarii Academiae Scientiarum Petropolitanae 11 (1765), pp. 103–123 (published 1767).

LOOKING BACKTHE ESSENTIALS AT A GLANCE

BASE ANGLE THEOREM

isosceles ⇔ base angles equal

base angle $70^\circ$ → apex $40^\circ$

SIDES AND ANGLES

The larger angle lies opposite the longer side

$\beta$ largest → $b$ longest

TRIANGLE INEQUALITY

two sides together longer than the third

3, 4, 8 cm: no triangle

SPECIAL LINES

perpendicular bisectors → $U$ · angle bisectors → $I$ · altitudes → $H$ · medians → $S$

$U$: circumcircle, $I$: incircle, $S$: centroid
